book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

chapters.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy® Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

chapters.relation: Show writer David Weddle recounts how Ron Moore pushed him and Brad Thompson to abandon Star Trek-style expository dialogue and tell 'Act of Contrition' through flashbacks interleaved with the present, dramatizing Starbuck's guilt over passing Zak Adama on his flight test. He argues this unlocked a stream-of-consciousness mode — dreams, hallucinations, and memories flowing out of characters' inner emotional lives — that the series extended in episodes like 'Scar,' 'Maelstrom,' and 'Unfinished Business,' echoing Faulkner's 'the past isn't even past.' The foreword is a creator's testimony that BSG's scrambled-chronology storytelling is what made the show worthy of a book of philosophical readings.

chapters.file: ch06 - “I Dare You to Watch This Show!”.md
chapters.relation: Editor Josef Steiff's introduction traces Galactica from Glen Larson's 1978 series and Galactica 1980 through the Moore/Eick re-imagining, and frames the show through Edward James Olmos's campus talks, where he 'dares' audiences to watch a series he calls truth about identity, race, culture, and purpose. It endorses Orson Scott Card's claim that true science fiction, like religious literature, asks who we are, what our place in the universe is, and how we find or make meaning. It closes by explaining the book's Cylon naming conventions (Sixes, Eights, Boomers, Athenas) and its gimmick of five unattributed 'Final Five' chapters.

chapters.file: ch08 - MODEL ONE - Some Are Programmed to Think They Are Human.md

chapters.relation: Milsky uses Ricoeur and MacIntyre's narrative theory of personal identity to read the two Sharons: Boomer's fabricated human backstory suffers a 'factual disruption' when she shoots Adama, while Athena's 'disruption of belief' comes from falling in love with Helo. He argues such disruptions — also suffered by humans like Starbuck (recovered memories of abuse in 'Maelstrom'), Roslin (coming to believe she is Pythia's dying leader), and Helo — need not destroy identity, since narratives can be retold, as the Final Four do in 'Crossroads, Part 2' with Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh' speech. Third-party narratives (Six disowning Athena, the crew refusing to see Boomer as Boomer) show identity is partly socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy, with Boomer's blackouts resembling dissociative identity disorder.

Booth argues that the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across television and Internet, forcing viewers to actively construct the story — Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing only make full sense if you pieced the webisodes together — and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performed roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's amnesia in 'Water,' Hera's human-Cylon hybridity, and Tigh's choice in 'Crossroads' to actively construct who he will be. The payoff: there is no central location for the self, the narrative, or Cylonhood — each becomes whole only through active construction.

Cuddy asks how gamers relate to BSG videogame avatars — as an extension of the ego or a disposable other — using Freud's id/ego/superego to cast the avatar as a socially safe venue for reconciling forbidden desires (piloting a Cylon Raider) with the superego's demands. Against Rehak's claim that gamers simply drop the avatar when losing, he enlists Sartre: blaming the game or 'cheating' opponents is bad faith, a denial of the freedom to create one's own essence, with Lee's '33' debate about responsibility for the Olympic Carrier and Baltar's vacillation as in-show parallels. Sartre's facticity bounds the freedom — hard missions are fixed facts to deal with — so the gamer, like Adama's fleet, must take responsibility within limits.

The chapter reads Baltar's Head-Six (and Caprica Six's Head-Baltar) through the gothic Double and Doppelgänger tradition, re-imagined via dissociative identity disorder: Baltar splits off his guilt over the genocide into a female doppelgänger who lets him evade responsibility, as in 'Precipice' where he finds the execution order signed without any memory of signing it. It then links this doubling to Plato's Symposium myth of lovers as split halves seeking their other half, since Baltar cannot function without some version of Six. Its resolution is Aristotle's golden mean: virtue is not choosing one self over another but balancing extremes, for individuals and for humanity and its Double, the Cylons — with Hera as the embodied balance.

chapters.file: ch13 - No Reason to Get Excited.md
chapters.relation: After 'Crossroads, Part 2' revealed Anders, Foster, Tigh, and Tyrol as Cylons, the chapter argues we can know that we exist (Descartes' cogito) without knowing what we are, since even Boomer's Cylon-detection result — Baltar's lie about the green light — could itself be a dream, returning us to Descartes' whirlpool. Moore's common-sense realism fails against the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism / relevant alternatives (Dretske) lets Starbuck dismiss dreaming-hypotheses about a Viper but cannot dismiss the possibility that you are a sleeper Cylon in a world where anyone might be one. Following Hume, who escaped skeptical paralysis by dining and playing backgammon, Tigh's 'report to your stations' shows the only live option: carry on being the person you want to be.

chapters.file: ch14 - MODEL TWO - They Look Like Us Now.md
ch15 - This Has All Happened Before and It Will All Happen Again.md
chapters.relation: Rennes reads the miniseries opening — Six's kiss of death with the Armistice officer — through postcolonial theory: Vergès's 'colonial family romance,' in which the human metropole adopts Cylons as perpetually subordinate children, and Bhabha's ambivalence and mimicry ('almost the same, but not quite'). The humans police difference first by appearance (toaster, skin-job slurs; the Centurion reflected in Helo's toaster) and then by blood, but métissage — Hera, whom Roslin tries to abort and then hides — exposes the categories as social constructions, since as D'Anna says, 'This stuff all looks the same.' Hera's menace is that acknowledging her means acknowledging human complicity in creating Cylon slaves, collapsing the colonial romance ('happily never after').

chapters.file: ch16 - Who They Are or Who They Want to Be.md
chapters.relation: Harwood-Smith argues via Judith Butler's performativity that Cylons have no pre-cultural 'I': Six is female because she performs femininity, and performing humanity increasingly makes it real — sex being the catalyst that destabilized Athena, who switches sides, while Boomer never takes responsibility for shooting Adama and so remains a slave to her programming. The performance runs backward too: humans who sleep with Cylons (Baltar, Tyrol, Helo treated as a 'toaster lover') absorb self-doubt about their own humanity, against the Cartesian inner 'I' that Baltar, who remade himself from farm-boy Aerelon, clings to. Butler's thesis is vindicated: if preprogrammed machines can be changed by the roles they play, anybody could.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Secret Plot of ‘Baby Boomers’.md
chapters.relation: Chess proposes that BSG is 'a narrative about queer reproduction,' combining Haraway's cyborg with Butler's heteronormativity to coin 'technoqueer': Cylons embody fears that technology makes heterosexual reproduction unnecessary. Helo's 'I'm in love with a woman I know isn't a woman,' the 'you can't rape a machine' debate after the Pegasus assault, and download-resurrection as asexual reproduction all mark Cylons as queer others — yet the Cylons' obsession with conceiving Hera, paralleled with The L Word's Bette and Tina, shows them trapped between rejecting and emulating heteronormativity, farming human women at the Cylon 'Farm' while craving legitimate babies. Hera's birth terrifies Roslin because it legitimizes the technoqueer and with it human reproductive obsolescence.

Heinricy argues the human/Cylon line is drawn on the body: following Mary Douglas, bodies function as cultural boundaries, so Cylons figure as contamination to be hunted (Boomer in the fleet) and marked as other by violence (Gina's torture), though Athena's loyal service and Tigh's exposure show the fear is socially constructed rather than natural. Cylon insides are known only through technology (Caprica Six's glowing spine, Athena's blood interface in 'Flight of the Phoenix'), and their bodies' stability — no scars, aging, or change — is paid for in unstable minds (Tigh killing Ellen, Boomer strangling Hera), whereas messy human bodies carry potential, hope, and change, as Apollo's weight fluctuation shows. Since we are all already cyborgs (vaccines, pills, GMOs), the Numbers are a further human-machine integration, and Hera and Nicky's blending is the ultimate 'contamination' and a new hope.

Hanley dismantles the four claimed human/Cylon differences: artificial reproduction is in principle possible for us; prosthetics already blur what we are made of; model copies differ like identical twins (Boomer is not Athena); and resurrection has human analogues — he proposes an SDTR (scanning, death, transmission, replication) model and uses van Inwagen's replica-switch account of bodily resurrection while rejecting soul-based reincarnation on Lockean grounds, since consciousness rather than soul is the criterion of identity. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction, not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), and reads Athena's memories of Tyrol as evidence she is a replicated Boomer. The upshot: being a Cylon is nothing to fear — 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'

chapters.file: ch20 - MODEL THREE - We Became What We Beheld.md

chapters.relation: Kind asks whether humanoid Cylons have moral status, using Warren's stone-versus-child contrast to show that the Fleet's blender-and-toaster attitude (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine') rests on the unargued assumption that Cylons are mere machines. Singer's anti-speciesism grounds status in sentience (Gina's suffering, even Scar the Raider), while Regan's subject-of-a-life criteria are met by rational, self-aware Cylons; Helo's 'no human could do the things they've done' argument fails because humans commit equal evils, as the legal limits on punishing criminals show. Since we cannot rule Cylon status out, she closes with Pascal's Wager: treat them as morally considerable, because the asymmetry of error costs us our moral compass.

Tamplin defends democracy through the Baltar election: Roslin's attempted theft failed, the voters' bad choice produced the New Caprica occupation, and this is exactly what Plato and Aristotle predicted of democracy as the deviant rule of the many, contrasted with Aristotle's polity aimed at the common advantage and a virtue 'every city' must care for. A thought experiment — an infallible computer advising citizens on every choice — shows that following it would abolish democracy, whose value lies not in results but in Aristotle's freedom, 'living as one wants.' Only by being allowed to frak things up can citizens learn from their mistakes, the road Apollo points to in his 'Crossroads' trial speech about collective shame, which is why Baltar's acquittal is a good sign.

Livingston reads the Razor movie through George Lakoff's Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models: Cain's Pegasus assumes a dangerous world and enforces obedience (shooting Belzen for refusing orders, the torture of Gina), while Adama's Galactica assumes empathy and open questioning (asking Boomer 'Why do you hate us so much?', sparing Starbuck). Kendra Shaw is the 'child' conditioned by desensitization and objectifying language into a killing razor and a PTSD victim, whose recovery under Apollo shows the two family models being blended — boldness with communication. Adama's verdict that 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain requires seeing the family culture that produced her.

chapters.file: ch24 - It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life.md
chapters.relation: Shipman argues that the re-imagined Cylons, having rebelled as slaves, recreated oppression inside their own society: the human-form Numbers rule over mute Centurions (voices literally bred out, like banning slave literacy), animalized Raiders, and dismissed 'insane' Hybrids, whose sentience ('Scar' shows strategy and self-preservation) the Numbers willfully deny. The division of labor echoes Marx's 'from each according to his ability,' but assignments are engineered by their makers, and the model-making program is eugenics rather than evolution — the series' own word 'evolved' is, he says, disingenuous. Hence the Numbers lose the moral superiority their victimhood earned, and the scriptural 'all of this has happened before' implies the subaltern models may rebel next.

Gray asks whether Cylons deserve moral consideration, starting from Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means: the New Caprica suicide bombings and Adama's plan to weaponize a Cylon virus treat captives merely as means, while Helo's sabotage of 'A Measure of Salvation' acknowledges their intrinsic value. D'Anna's dissent before being boxed and Athena's defection for Helo show the rational autonomy Kant's personhood requires; if that is dismissed as programming, Singer's sentience criterion (Leoben tortured, Gina catatonic) and Warren's multi-criterial personhood — including Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded' — still open personhood to Cylons. The chapter ends on the humans' double standard (Athena accepted, guns drawn on Caprica Six) as a mirror for our own treatment of uncertain others.

Pinedo argues the series restages 'blowback' — the CIA term for covert intervention rebounding on the intervener — in science-fiction guise: Adama's 'playing God' speech, the 'Hero' revelation that his Armistice Line black op (abandoning Bulldog Novacek) may have triggered the Cylon attack, and his confession 'I started it,' complicated by Roslin's warning against simple explanations. The sci-fi 'smokescreen' lets Moore and Eick critique the war on terror — torture, the Pegasus rapes, sympathetic suicide bombers — without naming blowback in a corporate media environment, as the producers' interviews and podcast commentaries show. The show refuses Manichean demonology: the Cylons are made in our image, and the capacity for evil 'is part of what we do in the name of war.'

Dinello reads the New Caprica occupation as an Iraq allegory interpreted through Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth: occupation is violence personified (Cavil's 'saving them from damnation'), psychological violence colonizes minds (Leoben's manipulation of Starbuck, Jammer's recruitment into the New Caprica Police), and Tyrol's 'throw your body on the gears' strike speech channels Savio, Marx's seizing the means of production, and Marcuse on technology's repression. Fanon's thesis that anticolonial violence is a cleansing, liberating force is dramatized in Tigh's 'blood for blood,' the Temple massacre that recruits a thousand fighters, and Duck's suicide bombing — with Sartre's preface endorsing killing the oppressor and the ends-justify-means dispute between Tigh and Tyrol. The insurgency wins by not losing, as in Algeria and Vietnam, and the show is subversive because it makes viewers sympathize with the occupied.

Peters applies Sartre's occupied-France analysis from Existentialism Is a Humanism to 'The Resistance' webisodes: on New Caprica one can resist (Tyrol, Tigh), collaborate (Jammer joining the NCP), or do nothing (Duck staying home with Nora), each path a Sartrean project whose morality lies in choosing freely and living with the consequences. Jammer's execution for treason in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing after Nora's death dramatize the stakes — for Sartre, Duck's immorality lies in refusing to own the choice he made at the crossroads, and the Final Four revelation changes nothing since they chose as they believed themselves human. The chapter leaves open the Sartrean worry that wartime morality may simply be written by the winners.

holes.name: Narrative Identity (emplotment)
holes.what: Ricoeur and MacIntyre's theory that personal identity consists in the unified, emplotted story a person tells about their life, revisable in light of new facts.
holes.why: Chapter 9 builds its entire account of Boomer and Athena Sharon's identity crises on narrative identity, emplotment, and factual/belief disruptions, none of which taxonomy.json has a slug for.

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway)
holes.what: Donna Haraway's hybrid human-machine figure whose breakdown of the human/animal, human/machine, and physical/non-physical boundaries makes identity itself hybrid and constructed.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses the cyborg to explain the humanoid Cylons and Hera as hybrids whose loyalties and identities must be actively constructed.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose structural model divides the psyche into id, ego, and superego, and whose 'family romance' describes the child's imaginative replacement of its parents.
holes.why: Chapter 11's first half explains the gamer-avatar bond as Freudian reconciliation of id and superego, and Freud's family romance also anchors the frameworks of chapters 12 and 15.

holes.name: The Double / Doppelgänger
holes.what: The gothic motif (theorized by Otto Rank) of a split second self — a corporeal Double or ghostly Doppelgänger — expressing anxiety about identity and the struggle between good and evil within.
holes.why: Chapter 12's whole framework reads Head Six and Head Baltar as Double and Doppelgänger tied to dissociative identity disorder, a concept taxonomy.json lacks.

holes.name: Homi Bhabha
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist of ambivalence, mimicry ('almost the same, but not quite'), and hybridity between colonizer and colonized.
holes.why: Chapter 15 applies Bhabha's ambivalence and mimicry to explain why the humans can neither keep the Cylons other nor absorb Hera, the mixed child who menaces the colonial order.

holes.name: The Colonial Family Romance (métissage)
holes.what: Françoise Vergès's inversion of Freud's family romance: the colonizing 'parent' adopts colonized 'children' who must remain perpetually different and subordinate, with mixed-race offspring (métissage) as its site of fascination and anxiety.
holes.why: Chapter 15 structures its entire reading of human-Cylon relations, racial slurs, and Hera's threatened abortion around this romance and its collapse.

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway)
holes.what: Donna Haraway's hybrid organism-machine figure, used in feminist theory to dissolve fixed categories of gender, race, and species.
holes.why: Chapter 17 opens by defining the Cylons through Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' before building its 'technoqueer' reading of Cylon reproduction on it.

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway)
holes.what: The human-machine hybrid as a theoretical condition: per cyborg theory, humans are already cyborgs through vaccines, prosthetics, and medication.
holes.why: Chapter 18 ('I, Cyborg') argues humans are already cyborgs and the humanoid Cylons a further organic-technological integration, a framework taxonomy.json lacks.

holes.name: Purity and Danger (dirt as matter out of place)
holes.what: Mary Douglas's anthropological account of how cultures use the body and notions of dirt and contamination to police social boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable bodies.
holes.why: Chapter 18 reads Cylon-contamination fears, segregation analogies, and Gina's torture as boundary-marking in Douglas's sense, with no matching taxonomy slug.

holes.name: George Lakoff
holes.what: Cognitive linguist who maps political morality onto idealized Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models of the family as metaphors framing moral cognition.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads Cain's Pegasus and Adama's Galactica in Razor as opposed Strict Father and Nurturant Parent families, with Kendra Shaw caught between the two models.

holes.name: The Wretched of the Earth (decolonizing violence)
holes.what: Fanon's account of colonial occupation as systematic violence and of anticolonial violence as the cleansing, self-creating force by which the colonized reclaim their humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 28 interprets the New Caprica insurgency's strikes and suicide bombings through exactly this framework, but taxonomy.json only carries Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks.
